A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same model-merging study. The original experiments, equations, checkpoint lists, and appendix figures can be matched despite retitling and substantial additions. Text extraction and visual inspection support reliable comparison, including the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations across four base models and sixteen benchmarks, including merge-size comparisons, taskwise results, and hyperparameter ablations in Tables 1–3 and Appendices B–C.

after.justification: v2 reports retained and revised benchmark results, plus new normalization controls, task-vector alignment measurements, and domain-specific merging experiments in Appendices C–E.

M1.justification: The evaluated merging algorithms and their principal procedures remain unchanged. Appendix C documents normalization as an existing configuration and tests normalization/scaling variants; it does not introduce a new merging algorithm or establish a change to the original method implementation.

E1.justification: Appendix E adds a distinct evaluation scenario using curated medical and mathematical specialists for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B. It tests preservation of domain capabilities through within-domain and joint-domain merging. The original checkpoint pools and sixteen-benchmark coverage remain; the new task suites draw on subsets of existing benchmarks.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain Task Arithmetic, TIES-Merging, Model Stock, TSV-Merge, Iso-C, TA+SB, and TIES+SB. Appendix E reuses these methods with base-model and individual-expert references. Newly cited works do not become additional evaluated merging algorithms.

E3.justification: New protocols include a joint TIES density–scaling grid, normalization-disabled Task Arithmetic controls, extension of the normalized scaling sweep to λ=10, and three-expert domain merges versus six-expert joint merges. Revised main TIES/TIES+SB evaluations specify λ=0.1; v1 did not separately state their scaling coefficient.

E4.justification: Appendices C–E substantially expand tests of why merging succeeds or fails: normalization controls, scaling-versus-update-norm analyses, global and layerwise task-vector alignment, and structured domain-mixing comparisons. The original density and boosting-threshold sweeps are retained as Figures 17 and 18, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions use fifteen matched checkpoint subsets at intermediate merge sizes, one all-twelve merge, and standard deviations across sampled subsets. No new seed-reporting practice, confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run uncertainty procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: TIES and TIES+SB results are substantially replaced. At n=12, the average success-rate/reported-improvement entries change from 0/-4.32 to 75/+0.13 in Table 1 and from 0/-8.67 to 100/+0.36 in Table 3. These are revised evaluations, not established gains under identical settings. Appendices C–E also add normalization, alignment, and domain-retention findings.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(11) are retained. Equation (12) spells out the weighted-average normalization that v2 says was already enabled. This implementation explanation and the qualitative cancellation arguments do not introduce a substantive theoretical derivation, formal assumption, theorem, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion narrow the central claim from merging methods generally failing to transfer to LLMs to difficulty improving general capabilities through heterogeneous, potentially conflicting checkpoints. TIES is recast from catastrophic degradation to limited gains under tuning. Task Arithmetic remains the preferred approach.

C2.justification: New explanations attribute Task Arithmetic’s stability to normalized averaging and TIES’s sensitivity to trimming and sign consensus limiting cancellation. Section 5 interprets the domain controls as evidence about heterogeneity, while Section 3.1 explicitly frames Model Stock’s use as a stress test beyond its intended setting. These materially revise mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v1’s promised code release becomes a repository link in v2. Appendices C and F newly disclose normalization, float16 evaluation, automatic batching, absence of chat templates, and exact few-shot counts. Appendix E supplies specialist checkpoint identifiers and task lists. These materially improve documentation without establishing that newly disclosed inference settings changed.

R1.justification: v2 removes the assertion that merging methods had not been evaluated on LLMs and distinguishes its general-capability objective from prior domain-specialist retention studies. New references include He et al.’s MergeBench, Cohere et al.’s Command A, and Roth et al. This substantially changes positioning; publication updates to retained references are bibliographic changes only.

P1.justification: The abstract and much of the introduction are rewritten, research questions are reformulated, and results, discussion, and conclusion narratives are revised around in-the-wild merging. Appendix C becomes a structured explanation with four subsections, and new appendices and a broader-impact statement extend the document structure.

P2.justification: v2 adds normalization and joint-sensitivity plots, global and layerwise alignment heatmaps, domain-comparison bar charts, and Tables 4–6. Figure 11 gains an extended scaling axis; retained displays are resized or relocated, and Table 2’s caption is expanded. Earlier density and boosting figures remain under new numbering.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central comparison by investigating scaling and normalization behind the earlier TIES failures, reporting tuned results, and narrowing broad LLM-failure claims to heterogeneous merging. Domain controls and explicit implementation/evaluation details improve evidential support and reproducibility. Section 5 still overstates causal certainty when attributing failures specifically to heterogeneity, but the correction of the central comparison and its interpretation provides a substantial net improvement.
